blocks.content: docker start brings an already-existing, stopped container back to running, reusing its exact same writable layer rather than creating anything new.
1. It Reuses, It Does Not Recreate
blocks.text: 1. It Reuses, It Does Not Recreate

blocks.content: The key thing to understand about docker start is that it operates on a container that already exists, one previously stopped, and simply resumes it. Nothing about the container's identity, its ID, its writable layer, its configuration, changes.

blocks.alt: The exact same container, running again

blocks.content:
docker ps -a                # find a stopped container's ID
docker start a1b2c3d4        # bring that same container back up

blocks.content: 2. How This Differs from docker run
blocks.text: 2. How This Differs from docker run

blocks.content: This is the flip side of the earlier docker exec vs docker run distinction: docker run always creates a brand new container, while docker start always resumes an existing one. Confusing the two is a common source of "why do I have five containers named web1 through web5" surprises.

blocks.alt: run always makes something new, start never does

blocks.content: Because docker start reuses the same container rather than creating a fresh one, any files that were written into the container's writable layer before it stopped are still there when it starts again, this is genuinely different from starting a new container from the same image, which would begin with an empty writable layer.

blocks.alt: Files written before stopping are still there afterward

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: docker start resumes an existing, stopped container exactly as it was, it never creates a new one, that is docker run's job.
A restarted container keeps whatever it had written to its writable layer before stopping, unlike a freshly run new container.
